'''David Leslie Hawksworth''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|CBE}} (born 1946 in Sheffield, UK) is a British [[mycologist]] and [[lichenologist]] currently with a professorship in the [[Universidad Complutense de Madrid]] in [[Madrid]], [[Spain]] and also a Scientific Associate of [[The Natural History Museum in London]]. Hawksworth has had a prolific career, authoring nearly 600 scientific works (including almost 60 books), [[species description|describing]] approximately 250 new [[taxon|taxa]], and proposing around 500 [[new combination]]s or new names in fungal nomenclature.<ref name="Lücking et al. 2020"/> In 1996, he was honoured as [[Commander of the British Empire]] (CBE).<ref name="Lücking et al. 2020"/> In 2002, he received the [[Acharius Medal]] from the [[International Association for Lichenology]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Acharius Medallists|url=http://www.lichenology.org/index.html?/Awards/AchariusMedallists.html|website=International Association for Lichenology|access-date=31 August 2015|archive-date=24 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624065615/http://www.lichenology.org/index.html?%2FAwards%2FAchariusMedallists.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Five [[genus|genera]] and many [[species]] have been named in his honour.

Hawksworth's research has focused on broad nomenclatural issues, fostering the integration of fungal nomenclature, and global assessment of fungal [[biodiversity|diversity]]. He has conducted systematic revisions of neglected groups, including [[lichenicolous fungus|lichenicolous]] taxa and fungi at the [[borderline lichen|borderline of lichenisation]], with a particular interest in the family [[Parmeliaceae]].<ref name="Lücking et al. 2020"/> From 1983 to 1997, Hawksworth served as director of the [[International Mycological Institute]] (IMI), overseeing its name change to Commonwealth Mycological Institute in 1986 and its move from [[Kew]] to [[Egham]] in 1993.<ref name="Lücking et al. 2020"/>

He married [[Patricia Wiltshire]], a leading [[forensic biology|forensic ecologist]] and [[palynologist]] in 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.lichenology.org/Awards/Acharius_Hawksworth.html |title=Biography at lichenology.org |access-date=17 August 2009 |archive-date=19 July 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070719235500/http://www.lichenology.org/Awards/Acharius_Hawksworth.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> {{as of|2022}}, he is the Editor-in-Chief of the journals ''[[IMA Fungus]]''<ref>{{cite web |url=https://imafungus.biomedcentral.com/about/editorial-board |title=IMA Fungus - The global mycological journal, Editorial Board |website=IMA Fungus |access-date=20 August 2022}}</ref> and ''[[Biodiversity and Conservation]]''.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.springer.com/journal/10531 |title=Biodiversity and Conservation | publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media]] |access-date=20 August 2022}}</ref>

==Education==

Born in [[Sheffield]] in 1946, David Hawksworth studied at the [[University of Leicester]]. From this institution, he earned a [[BSc]] in 1967, a [[PhD]] in 1970, and a [[DSc]] in 1980.<ref name="Kärnefelt 2009"/>

==Career reflections==

In a 2020 article reflecting on his 50-year career in mycology, Hawksworth shared ten key lessons he had learnt as a fungal [[systematics|systematist]]. Among these, he emphasised the importance of thorough research before [[species description|describing]] new taxa, stressing that it is far easier to introduce a new name than to determine if a fungus has already been described. Hawksworth advocated for examining as many specimens as possible to understand species variation and utilising a wide range of techniques to study fungal characteristics.<ref name="Hawksworth 2020"/>

Hawksworth highlighted the significance of careful microscopic examination and measurement of fungal structures, noting the potential impact of different mounting media on spore sizes. He encouraged mycologists to challenge existing ideas and present new hypotheses, citing his own work in integrating lichen-forming fungi into a single [[classification (biology)|classification]] system with other fungi. Another key lesson stressed the importance of preserving [[type (biology)|type specimens]] and vouchers for unusual records to ensure the validity of taxonomic work.<ref name="Hawksworth 2020"/>

Throughout his career, Hawksworth has been at the forefront of adopting new technologies in mycological research. He was among the first in the UK to use [[chromatography]], [[scanning electron microscopy]], and [[numerical taxonomy]] in the [[systematics]] of lichen-forming fungi. Hawksworth has also been a proponent of [[molecular phylogenetics|molecular]] methods in fungal taxonomy, collaborating with other researchers to address key questions in the field. He emphasised the value of teamwork in modern mycology, noting that multi-authored papers have become the norm in addressing complex research questions.<ref name="Hawksworth 2020"/>

==Recognition==

In 1978, Hawksworth received the [[Bicentenary Medal of the Linnean Society]].<ref name="Hawksworth 2014"/> He was awarded an [[honorary doctorate]] from the [[Umeå University]] in 1996.<ref name="Kärnefelt 2009"/> In 2014, Hawksworth was awarded the Ainsworth Medal from the [[International Mycological Association]], given to "an individual for recognition of extraordinary service to world mycology".<ref name="Hawksworth 2014"/>

In 2020, on the occasion of David Hawksworth's 70th birthday, [[Robert Lücking]] and colleagues described 70 new species of lichenised [[basidiomycete]] fungi in the genus ''[[Cora (fungus)|Cora]]'', many of which were [[eponym|named in his honour]]. This represented the largest number of new species ever described in a single publication for lichens. The authors devised creative variations on Hawksworth's name for the [[botanical name|species epithets]], including:<ref name="Lücking et al. 2020"/>

*Direct references like ''[[Cora hawksworthiana|C.&nbsp;hawksworthiana]]'' and ''[[Cora davidia|C.&nbsp;davidia]]''
*[[Anagram]]s such as ''[[Cora dalehana|C.&nbsp;dalehana]]'' and ''[[Cora viliewoa|C.&nbsp;viliewoa]]''
*References to the meaning or origin of his name, like ''[[Cora accipiter|C.&nbsp;accipiter]]'' ("hawk")
*Plays on his initials DLH, as in ''[[Cora hochesuordensis|C.&nbsp;hochesuordensis]]''
*Allusions to places associated with the Hawksworth name, e.g. ''[[Cora hafecesweorthensis|C.&nbsp;hafecesweorthensis]]''

The paper and mass-naming event highlighted Hawksworth's significant contributions to mycology and lichenology over his career. It also demonstrated the previously unrecognised [[biodiversity]] in the genus ''Cora'', which Hawksworth had earlier worked on nomenclaturally.<ref name="Lücking et al. 2020"/>
